Lesson 9 · Technical continuation

How much did alerts help those stores?

The same stores, calculation, and decision—with the specification and reproducible steps visible.

Voluntary cohort · S051–S100 · outcome weeks 17–24

← Return to the worked analysis

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

Use the same analysis rows

The outcome model uses columns [1, D, lead−3.5, urban, baseline_rate, D×(lead−3.5), D×urban]. Fit by least squares on one post-period mean per store. The centered lead variable makes the treatment coefficient refer to a stated delivery-time value.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

For each target row construct X0 and X1 by setting D to zero or one, including the interaction terms. The estimated reduction is (X0−X1)β. Average those row vectors for the target population before calculating the standard error.

w = world()
post = w['panel'].query('cohort == \"Voluntary\" and 17 <= week <= 24')
v = post.groupby('store_id').agg(rate=('stockout_rate','mean')).reset_index()
v = v.merge(w['stores'][['store_id','offer','lead_days','urban','baseline_rate']], on='store_id')
X = voluntary_design(v, v.offer.to_numpy())
beta, covariance, residual = fit_ols(X, v.rate)
X0 = voluntary_design(v, np.zeros(len(v)))
X1 = voluntary_design(v, np.ones(len(v)))
paired_reductions = (X0-X1) @ beta
worked_effect = paired_reductions.mean()
assert np.isclose(worked_effect, lesson_result(9)['estimate'])

# Estimate adoption propensities using only starting conditions.
w = world()
voluntary = w['panel'].query("cohort=='Voluntary' and 17<=week<=24")
v = voluntary.groupby(['store_id','offer']).stockout_rate.mean().reset_index()
v = v.merge(w['stores'][['store_id','lead_days','urban','baseline_rate']],
    on='store_id',validate='one_to_one')
covariates = ['lead_days','urban','baseline_rate']
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(C=1.,max_iter=1000))
model.fit(v[covariates],v.offer)
propensity = model.predict_proba(v[covariates])[:,1]
v['logit'] = np.log(propensity/(1-propensity))
caliper = .2*v.logit.std(ddof=1)
controls = v[v.offer==0]
matched_effects = []
for adopter in v[v.offer==1].itertuples():
    # Numerically tied distances use the lowest store ID.
    closest = nearest_score_match(controls,adopter.logit)
    comparison = controls.loc[closest]
    if abs(comparison.logit-adopter.logit)<=caliper:
        matched_effects.append(comparison.stockout_rate-adopter.stockout_rate)
assert np.isclose(np.mean(matched_effects),lesson_result(9)['depth']['matching'][2]['estimate'])

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

The reported covariance is HC1: (X′X)⁻¹ X′diag(e²)X (X′X)⁻¹ × n/(n−p). With average contrast c, the standard error is √(c′Vc). The interval uses the normal 1.96 multiplier. It is uncertainty for the chosen outcome model and target.

Change one analytical choice

Nearest-neighbor matching standardizes the three pre-policy variables by their full-cohort standard deviations and uses squared Euclidean distance. Matching is with replacement and targets adopters. Inspect repeated controls and the pre-policy distances when comparing it with the model.

Reproduce the matching choices

Nearest-neighbor covariate matching in the core calculation uses standardized squared distance with replacement. Exact matching and coarsened matching use stratum comparison means. Propensity matching uses a fitted logistic score, nearest neighbors on its logit, and the stated caliper. Distances within 1e-10 of the minimum are treated as numerical ties and resolved by the lowest store ID. These procedures can estimate different retained populations even when all are described as matching.

Standardized mean difference = (treated mean − comparison mean) / pooled pre-match SD

The table does not attach a naive independent-observation interval to reused comparison records. Estimated scores, selection of matches, and reuse affect uncertainty. Inspect the saved match counts, balance measures, and regression specification before selecting a procedure for the decision.

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0 = 0.055 + 0.014 × lead + 0.0005 × (demand − 100) + 0.018 × urban + 0.003 × (lead − 3) × urban + 0.020 × promotion + store effect + 0.006 × sin(week / 4)

Expected reduction = 0.006 + 0.008 × lead + 0.004 × urban; p1 = p0 − reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.

Read the shared generator and analysis source

Compare with the known answer

The known expected reduction for all 50 stores is 3.34 points; for their adopters it is 3.65. Comparing estimates with the matching target separates estimation error from a change in population.
